transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump is facing scathing criticism over remarks he made during a campaign stop
in Nebraska while talking about the increase in gas prices resulting from the Iran war.
Trump seemed to suggest that allowing Iran to take out Los Angeles or San Diego would
be a small price to pay compared to the war's eventual benefits.
Steve Futterman has reaction from Los Angeles.
Officials here in California are strongly criticizing the president.
Governor Gavin Newsom on social media called Trump "deranged and dangerous."
Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass also had a strong response.
"You don't say things like that.
You're the president of the United States."
She told NPR irresponsible there's not a strong enough word to describe the comments.
"It's just frightening that a president of the United States would basically call on
a foreign power to attack the nation's second largest city."
San Diego mayor Todd Gloria said his city is not collateral damage and is not expendable.
He told the president to keep San Diego out of his reckless war talk.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman in Los Angeles.
Massive student protest marches are being held in Paris and other French cities.
The movement for better conditions in high schools is now in its second week.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley is with protesters as they gathered in Paris.
They're all singing the Marseillaise.
The students have climbed up the Republique statue and they're singing in unison with
their signs right ahead of their march today.
Tens of thousands of students are gathering here in Place de la Republique.
They say that this is the strongest student movement in decades.
They're even comparing it to May 1968, which brought down the government of President Charles
de Gaulle.
That's NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reporting.
A professor in Wisconsin has been recognized for his work scoping out so-called ghost particles.
Sarah Lear of Wisconsin Public Radio has more on the latest winner of the Nobel Prize in
Physics.
Neutrinos are nearly massless astrophysical particles.
They're key to understanding black holes, galaxies, and other mysterious parts of the
cosmos, but they're notoriously difficult to detect.
Francis Halzen, a Belgian-born scientist, came up with an idea.
Sometimes neutrinos put out flashes of light, which he thought could be glimpsed using sensors
and clear glacial ice.
That led the University of Wisconsin-Madison to build its Ice Cube telescope at the South
Pole.
Turns out, those doubters were wrong, and now, at 82 years old, Halzen has a Nobel Prize
to show for his work.
For NPR News, I'm Sarah Lear in Madison, Wisconsin.
The U.S. stock market hit an all-time high today as expectations rose for companies to
keep making more money.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Attorneys for Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee's attempt to execute her last week, say she
is awake and speaking in a hospital, her attorneys say they are grateful for the medical team
who "treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her."
Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital, as Tennessee officials attempted to put her
to death.
A public comment period is wrapping up on the Trump administration's plan to reverse
a ban on logging in national forests, and PR's Kirk Sigler reports the so-called "roadless
rule" dates back to the Clinton administration.
The Trump administration wants to overturn the roadless rule that bans new road building
on millions of acres of undeveloped national forest land, areas that had been set aside
for possible wilderness designations.
Travis Joseph with the Timber Group American Forest Resource Council says that rule is
outdated.
This is a 25-year-old administrative policy passed by an administration, not by Congress,
and the Constitution gives Congress the power to make the laws and regulations that govern
public land.
Conservationists argue the rule is one of the only tools left to protect critical wildlife
and watersheds in Alaska and the West.
A final decision on its repeal is expected later this year.
Kirk Sigler, NPR News.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Quebec should focus on immediate economic challenges
rather than a possible independence referendum years from now.
Yesterday, separatist party Québécois returned to power as Canada confronts President Trump's
tariffs and repeated threats against the country.
Meanwhile, Alberta is holding a vote to secede from Canada later this month.
I'm Rylan Barton, this is NPR News from Washington.
Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks?
Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News now, sponsor free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism and get NPR+ at plus.npr.org.
That's plus dot NPR dot org.

topics.text: President Trump faces criticism over remarks suggesting Iran attack on Los Angeles or San Diego acceptable
California officials including Governor Newsom and Mayor Bass condemn Trump's comments about potential Iran attacks
San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria says city is not collateral damage in Trump's war rhetoric
Massive student protest marches held in Paris and French cities demanding better high school conditions
University of Wisconsin professor Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in Physics for neutrino detection work
U.S. stock market hits all-time high as company profit expectations rise
Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee execution attempt, awake and speaking in hospital
Trump administration plans to reverse Clinton-era roadless rule banning logging roads in national forests
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urges Quebec to focus on economic challenges over independence
Separatist Québécois party returns to power in Quebec as Alberta considers secession vote
